explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The wise say, "To show partiality in judgment is not good." A judge who leans toward his buddy is like a cookie scale that adds a thumb on one side. Everybody who walks in deserves the same fair measure.

Not this one, friend. The saying never mentions how long a judge takes. It says, "To show partiality in judgment is not good." That means playing favorites, and a slow judge who treats everyone the same is still being fair.

Not quite, friend. Nothing in this saying says a hard question is a problem. What the wise call not good is this: "To show partiality in judgment is not good." Hard questions asked of everybody alike sound pretty fair to me.

I see why you'd think so, friend, but it's the other way around. The text says that whoever tells the guilty, "You are innocent…" will have peoples curse him and nations denounce him. No applause and no parade. Just a whole lot of people upset with him.

That's right, friend. The one who tells the guilty "You are innocent…" gets cursed by peoples and denounced by nations. That's a LOT of people lined up against one fella. I'd rather give an honest answer and keep my friends.

Yes, friend. The text says it will go well with those who convict the guilty, and "…rich blessing will come upon them." Notice that it's the opposite of what happens to the one who calls the guilty innocent. Telling the truth when it's hard has a payoff.
I get it, friend. Speaking up against wrong can feel risky. But the text says, "…rich blessing will come upon them." It's the one who calls the guilty innocent who ends up cursed and denounced.

Speaking up can feel heavy, friend, I get that. But the saying promises blessing: it will go well with those who convict the guilty, and "…rich blessing will come upon them." Sorrow isn't what that verse says comes upon them.
That's it, friend. "An honest answer given is like a kiss on the lips." That's a warm, close picture. An honest word treats you like someone worth being straight with.

I can see how honesty might feel like that sometimes, friend. But the wise picked something warmer: "An honest answer given is like a kiss on the lips." No sword in this saying. Just a close, caring picture.
Cold water sounds nice, friend, and Proverbs does use it elsewhere (Proverbs 25:25). But here the wise say, "An honest answer given is like a kiss on the lips." That's the picture for this saying.

Other way around, friend. The saying says, "Complete your outdoor work and prepare your field; after that, you may build your house." Field first, house after. Building the house first is like hanging curtains before the walls are up.

Right, friend. The wise say, "Complete your outdoor work and prepare your field; after that, you may build your house." The field comes first and the house comes after. Get the outdoor work done, and then go build.

Yes, friend. The saying says, "Do not testify against your neighbor without cause…" The trouble is speaking against him when there's no reason for it. A witness is supposed to tell what's true, not just what's handy.

Not this one, friend. Nothing in the saying says where the testimony happens, whether it's a public square or the parking lot. It says, "Do not testify against your neighbor without cause…" The missing cause is what the warning is about.
Plot twist, friend, but no relatives show up in this one. Not even a cousin gets a cameo. The saying says, "Do not testify against your neighbor without cause…" The cause is what's missing.

That's right, friend. The same verse says, "Do not testify against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips." Both warnings sit right together. Your mouth is supposed to be honest, whether it's in court or around the neighbor's fence.

It's actually in there, friend. Verse 28 says, "Do not testify against your neighbor without cause, and do not deceive with your lips." Both warnings are in one verse. Deceiving with your lips doesn't get to hide in a different saying.

Tempting, friend, I know. But the wise say, "Do not say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work.”" That's a no. The comeback you rehearsed in the shower can stay in the shower.

That's right, friend. The text says, "Do not say, “I will do to him as he has done to me; I will repay the man according to his work.”" Getting even is exactly what the wise tell us not to say. It's hard to hear, I know.
Nope, friend. The writer says, "Thorns had grown up everywhere, thistles had covered the ground…" Thorns everywhere, so they haven't been cleared away. That's the opposite of a tidy field.
That's right, friend. The text says, "Thorns had grown up everywhere, thistles had covered the ground…" Everywhere, not just one corner. That's a field nobody's been looking after.
Yes, friend. The text says, "…the stone wall was broken down." Thorns inside and a wall that fell apart outside. Nobody's been taking care of that place.
I wish, friend, but no. The verse says, "…the stone wall was broken down." A freshly built wall would mean somebody's been working. This field has the opposite problem.
Interesting guess, friend. But the text doesn't say anybody started building. It says, "…the stone wall was broken down." That's a wall that fell apart, not one waiting to be finished.
Yes, friend. The writer says, "I observed and took it to heart; I looked and received instruction…" He didn't just walk past. He looked at that field and learned something from it.
Ha, nobody's paying anybody for looking at thorns, friend. The writer says, "I observed and took it to heart; I looked and received instruction…" What he walked away with was a lesson.
Kind of you to think of it, friend, but thanks isn't what the writer got. He says, "I observed and took it to heart; I looked and received instruction…" He got a lesson out of what he saw.

That's right, friend. The writer says, "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest…" Little, little, little. And then the next verse says "…poverty will come upon you like a robber…"
Look again, friend. The warning really is about "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest…" Each one sounds small. That's the whole trick of it.

Yes, friend. The writer says, "…poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit." A robber doesn't knock first. It can feel like it came out of nowhere, but it's those little rests piling up.
Not this one, friend. Sickness and storms aren't in this verse. It says, "…poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit." The warning is about running short.
Good try, friend, but shame and floods aren't in this saying. The text says, "…poverty will come upon you like a robber, and need like a bandit." That's what follows all the little rests.
